slide.title: Is Deep Learning Worth It?
slide.body: Left: simple icon of a table with columns. Right: icon of a photo feeding into layered nodes and a GPU chip. Small tag: Deep Learning and Neural Networks · Lesson 1.

scenes.on_screen_text: When is deep learning worth it?
scenes.voiceover: You can already get a strong result from a gradient-boosted model on a clean table in a few minutes. So why spend hours training a neural network on a GPU? Sometimes, you should not. Let's see when deep learning is worth the cost.

slide.title: Why Deep Learning?
slide.body: Deep Learning and Neural Networks · Lesson 1 of 20

scenes.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to Deep Learning and Neural Networks. In this first lesson, we decide when deep learning makes sense, and we get a GPU ready.

slide.title: Classical ML: meaningful features
slide.body: Logistic regression · random forests · gradient boosting. Columns already mean something: age · income · late payments. A person does the feature engineering.

scenes.voiceover: The classical models from the scikit-learn course, such as random forests and gradient boosting, work on features that already mean something. Age, income, the number of late payments. A person does most of the work by building those features.

slide.title: A photo is just numbers
slide.body: A 224×224 colour photo → zoom into a grid of pixel values → label: about 150,000 numbers, none of them means 'cat'.

scenes.voiceover: Images, audio and text are different. A colour photo of two hundred and twenty-four by two hundred and twenty-four pixels is about one hundred and fifty thousand numbers. No single pixel means leaf disease or cat.

slide.title: Representation learning
slide.body: Four boxes left to right, one per layer: edges → textures → shapes → objects. Caption: the network learns features from raw data.

scenes.voiceover: The useful features are patterns of patterns. Edges, then textures, then shapes, then objects. A neural network learns these features directly from the raw data, layer by layer. This is called representation learning, and it is why deep learning works so well on unstructured data.

slide.title: The cost is real
slide.body: Data: more labelled examples (unless pretrained, L10, L13) · Compute: a GPU helps a lot · Tuning and debugging: more ways to fail (L08, L15) · Explainability: harder to say why

scenes.voiceover: But the cost is real. Networks usually need more labelled data, unless you start from a pretrained model. They need more compute. They have more settings to tune and more ways to fail. And it is harder to explain why they made a decision.

scenes.on_screen_text: Deep learning also learns the measurements
scenes.voiceover: Here is a way to picture it. Classical machine learning is like a skilled tailor who works from measurements someone else has taken. Deep learning is a tailor who also learns to take the measurements from photos. More flexible, but slower to learn.

slide.title: A practical rule
slide.body: Small or medium tables → tree-based model first. Images, audio, text → pretrained network. GPU: thousands of parallel operations, ideal for matrix multiplication.

scenes.voiceover: So, a practical rule. On small or medium tables, try a tree-based model first. On images, audio or text, start with a pretrained network. And why a GPU? It runs thousands of simple calculations in parallel, which is exactly what matrix multiplication inside every layer needs.

Meet Dilnoza, a data scientist at a textile company in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. Project A predicts late supplier deliveries from a table of eight thousand orders. Her gradient-boosting model already scores well, so she keeps it.

slide.title: Two projects, two choices
slide.body: Project A: 8,000 orders × 20 columns → keep gradient boosting. Project B: fabric photos, small holes and uneven threads → convolutional network, later transfer learning.

scenes.voiceover: Project B detects weaving faults in fabric photos. There are no useful columns, only pixels, and hand-made features miss small holes and uneven threads. That is a good case for a convolutional network. Let's prepare the GPU.

screen_steps: Open colab.research.google.com and click New notebook
Choose a GPU hardware accelerator and click Save
scenes.voiceover: Open a new Colab notebook. From the Runtime menu, choose Change runtime type, select a GPU hardware accelerator, and save.

screen_steps: Run the check cell: import torch, time; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available()); device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
scenes.voiceover: Now run the check cell. It prints the PyTorch version, and whether PyTorch can see a GPU. If it says true, you are ready. If it says false, the code still runs, but on the CPU, and slowly.

screen_steps: Run the timing cell from content.md: a = torch.randn(4096, 4096); time a @ a on CPU
Same cell: g = a.to(device); torch.cuda.synchronize(); time g @ g; torch.cuda.synchronize()
scenes.voiceover: Next, the timing cell. It creates a large random matrix of about four thousand by four thousand numbers, multiplies it by itself on the CPU, and then does the same on the GPU.

screen_steps: Run the timing cell a second time
Point to the second-run CPU and GPU times (expected output: GPU many times faster; exact numbers vary)
scenes.voiceover: Run it twice, because the first GPU run includes start-up time. On the second run, you should see something like a GPU that is many times faster. Exact numbers depend on your hardware.

screen_steps: Highlight both torch.cuda.synchronize() calls in the timing cell
scenes.voiceover: Notice the synchronise calls. GPU work runs in the background, so without them the timer stops too early.

scenes.on_screen_text: Choose by data type, not novelty
scenes.voiceover: One common mistake is to think deep learning is always better. On small tables, a well-tuned tree model is often just as accurate, faster and easier to explain. Choose deep learning because of the data, not because it is newer.

slide.title: Good to know
slide.body: Free GPU type and limits change · Colab not available everywhere · Every exercise also runs on CPU with a smaller subset · Fallback: local Jupyter notebook

scenes.voiceover: A quick note on access. Free GPU limits change and are not guaranteed, and Colab is not available everywhere. Every exercise in this course also finishes on a CPU with a smaller data subset, in Colab or a local notebook.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Networks learn features from unstructured data; on small tables, classical models often win. 2. Deep learning costs data, compute, tuning and explainability. 3. Check the GPU, choose a device, synchronise before timing.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, neural networks learn features from raw, unstructured data like images, audio and text. On small tables, classical models are often just as good and cheaper. Second, deep learning costs more data, compute, tuning and explanation, so choose it for a reason. Third, check for a GPU in PyTorch, choose a device for your tensors, and synchronise before timing GPU work.
